Affiliation: Renmin University of China Abstract Irregular All-to-All communication is a major bottleneck in expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Even with fixed expert routing and placement, uneven utilization of parallel network Rails and incast can limit communication performance. We present RailWave, a phase-adaptive communication layer built on DeepEP that addresses these bottlenecks below the routing layer through spatial and temporal traffic shaping. RailBalance redistributes source traffic across eligible Rails using source-local information, while a reusable, topology-derived permutation schedule limits concurrent senders per receiver without rebuilding demand-dependent schedules for each communication phase. A lightweight calibrated selector chooses an execution path according to each phase’s traffic characteristics and offline profiling results. On training-derived communication workloads from the 106B GLM-4.5-Air model, RailWave delivers up to 5.84 × 5.84\times speedup on H800 and 4.36 × 4.36\times on H20 over Native. Code is available at https://github.com/CyberSecurityErial/RailWave-EP . 1 Introduction Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models increase model capacity while activating only a subset of parameters for each token ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Lepikhin et al., 2021 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . Expert parallelism (EP) distributes experts across GPUs, requiring dispatch and combine exchanges between tokens and their selected experts. Because routing induces uneven and input-dependent traffic, these exchanges form irregular All-to-All communication and can become a major bottleneck in MoE execution ( Liao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . Existing approaches improve MoE efficiency through routing, expert placement, and replication ( Lewis et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ; Nie et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2022 ) . Replication-based methods can additionally incur per-layer memory overhead from redundant expert states ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . These mechanisms shape the logical communication demand, but do not fully determine its physical execution. This distinction is particularly important in Rail-optimized clusters, where a high-bandwidth intra-node fabric connects multiple scale-out paths ( NVIDIA, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Even with an optimized dispatch–combine backend such as DeepEP ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , traffic can still be redistributed across eligible Rails and node-pair transfers can overlap in different orders. These execution choices expose two bottlenecks, as shown in Figure 1 : (a) Balanced expert and destination-node loads can coexist with concentrated source-Rail traffic, leaving parallel paths underutilized. (b) Conversely, balanced source Rails do not prevent multiple senders from converging on the same receiver and creating incast. Our analysis of 900 training step–layer pairs further shows that expert-load imbalance has limited linear explanatory power for Rail imbalance. We therefore jointly control where traffic enters the scale-out network and which node-pair transfers overlap. (a) Rail imbalance (b) Receiver incast Figure 1: Two bottlenecks with fixed routing. (a) Balanced expert and destination-node loads can coexist with a hot source Rail. (b) Balanced source Rails can still feed the same receiver concurrently. We present RailWave, a communication layer built on DeepEP for spatial and temporal control of expert-parallel traffic. RailBalance redistributes outgoing traffic across eligible Rails using source-local information, without requiring destination-side balancing. Reusable topology-derived permutation scheduling organizes node-pair transfers into communication waves that bound incast degree without rebuilding a demand-dependent schedule for each phase. The two mechanisms are complementary: traffic that is balanced across Rails over an entire phase can become concentrated within an individual wave. RailWave therefore exposes four execution paths combining these mechanisms and uses a lightweight calibrated selector to choose among them according to the current traffic characteristics and validated offline profiling results. This work makes four contributions: • We present RailWave, a DeepEP-based communication layer for joint control of Rail allocation and node-pair overlap. • We design RailBalance, a source-local mechanism for shaping traffic across parallel Rails. • We adapt reusable topology-derived permutation scheduling to bound incast degree across changing routing phases. • We evaluate RailWave on two 32-GPU H800 and H20 clusters using real GLM-4.5-Air training workloads, achieving up to 5.84 × 5.84\times and 4.36 × 4.36\times communication speedups, respectively, over Native execution. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Expert-parallel communication Under EP, dispatch sends routed token representations to remote experts, and combine returns their outputs. Routing and expert placement determine the participants and volume of these irregular All-to-All exchanges. We consider an EP group spanning N N nodes. In one dispatch or combine operation, D s , d D_{s,d} denotes the traffic volume from source node s s to destination node d d . To examine the first distinction, we analyze routing records from 900 training step–layer pairs and derive Rail loads using the expert-to-Rail mapping. Figure 2 (a) selects six cases whose expert-load max/mean ratios lie between 8.2 8.2 and 8.4 8.4 . Their busiest destination-Rail assignment shares range from 15.5 % 15.5\% to 24.1 % 24.1\% . Across all records, linear fits from expert-load imbalance to source- and destination-Rail imbalance yield R 2 = 0.019 R^{2}=0.019 and 0.296 0.296 , respectively (Figure 2 (b)). Expert-load imbalance therefore has limited linear explanatory power for the observed Rail-load variation. Figure 2: Rail-load imbalance and incast under fixed routing. (a) Six cases with similar expert-load imbalance but different destination-Rail concentration; the two label rows identify training step and layer. (b) Linear fits over 900 training step–layer pairs. (c) Native latency under two replay orders with identical rank-to-rank demand. Figure 2 (c) quantifies the impact of incast on communication latency. We keep the rank-to-rank demand, payload, backend, and number of communication rounds fixed, while varying which node pairs transmit concurrently. The sum of per-layer P50 dispatch–combine latencies increases from 1.801 1.801 to 3.009 3.009 s, a 67.1 % 67.1\% increase. This result shows that the same rank-to-rank demand can incur higher communication latency under stronger incast. 2.4 MoE communication optimization MoE communication has been optimized at several layers of the software stack. Upper-layer methods change the demand presented to communication: EPLB, UltraEP, MoonEP, and TAOT adjust expert placement, replication, or token-to-replica assignment to balance expert or device loads ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . NetMoE adjusts input-sample placement to exploit network locality ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , while node-limited routing restricts the destinations selected for each token ( DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) . These decisions shape the logical demand matrix D D . RailWave operates after them and optimizes how the resulting communication is executed. EP communication libraries optimize the dispatch–combine data path across intra- and inter-node fabrics. DeepEP and NCCL-EP use high-bandwidth intra-node communication to stage or redistribute tokens before scale-out transmission ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Goldman et al., 2026 ) . SwiftEP reduces data-path overhead through buffer fusion and TMA offloading ( Li et al., 2026 ) , while UBEP combines finer-grained execution with topology-aware scheduling for high-bandwidth superpods ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . EPIC spans logical and physical optimization, coupling expert migration with topology-adaptive transport and communication–computation overlap ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . RailWave builds on DeepEP to control the Rail distribution and concurrent execution of the transfers carried by this backend. Network-aware mechanisms are the closest to RailWave. RailS and FuseLink primarily improve path utilization through local traffic redistribution ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) , whereas RailWave additionally controls which node-pair transfers overlap at a receiver. FAST explicitly balances traffic across the GPUs and NICs within each node, then uses demand-dependent Birkhoff scheduling to construct balanced one-to-one stages ( Lei et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . This planning requires a consistent view of source–destination demand across nodes; synchronizing that information and rebuilding schedules can incur substantial overhead as routing changes. RailWave instead reuses topology-derived cyclic peer plans with source-local RailBalance, reducing this coordination and plan-construction overhead. Rate-based scheduling controls incast through sender pacing ( Cohen et al., 2026 ) . SABRE selects communication strategies according to endpoint-volume skew ( Wei and Bhatele, 2026 ) , whereas RailWave indexes offline-calibrated path decisions by payload, global source-Rail skew, and receiver concentration. Other approaches reduce payload size or overlap communication with computation ( Nie et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . These optimizations are complementary to RailWave’s execution control. 3 System Design RailWave combines source-local Rail redistribution with node-pair scheduling on top of DeepEP. Figure 3 shows its three-stage workflow: preparation, selection, and execution. Offline profiling produces a cost table, while initialization constructs reusable peer plans from the EP topology. During execution, routing and window-derived traffic statistics feed a selector that chooses among Native , Rail-only , Permutation-only , and Joint . Native retains the backend execution path; Rail-only changes the egress allocation; Permutation-only changes which node pairs communicate concurrently; Joint applies RailBalance within each scheduled wave. The selector reuses validated offline decisions near calibrated operating points and otherwise falls back to Joint. The selected plan records the transfer order and owner-to-proxy mapping. Dispatch delivers the original expert inputs through this plan, and combine uses the saved metadata to return outputs to their original token positions. All ranks follow the same active execution path and wave order, and the selected plan remains fixed for the corresponding dispatch–combine pair. Figure 3: RailWave overview. Offline profiling and current-phase traffic statistics drive execution selection, while topology-derived peer plans are reused across phases. With N N nodes, wave k ∈ { 1 , … , N − 1 } k\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\} uses π k ​ ( s ) \displaystyle\pi_{k}(s) = ( s + k ) mod N , \displaystyle=(s+k)\bmod N, (10) π k − 1 ​ ( d ) \displaystyle\pi_{k}^{-1}(d) = ( d − k ) mod N . \displaystyle=(d-k)\bmod N. Each node has at most one outgoing and one incoming peer in a wave. Every remote ordered pair appears exactly once because its shift is uniquely determined by ( d − s ) mod N (d-s)\bmod N . These peer relationships depend only on group membership and are constructed once; each phase supplies new transfer records and counts. For a wave, the executor selects records whose destination is π k ​ ( s ) \pi_{k}(s) and packs their payload without padding the node-pair demand. This partition operates over backend transfer records, including multiple destinations for the same token. Within each backend invocation, DeepEP and Rail-only admit the submitted remote pairs together, whereas Permutation-only and Joint execute the cached peer plans in order. Within each wave, disjoint node pairs communicate concurrently. Joint applies RailBalance to the records in the current wave. A phase can be balanced across Rails in aggregate while a particular destination slice remains concentrated on a few Rails. Redistributing that slice can shorten the wave’s critical transfer. The gain depends on its Rail skew and relocation cost; scheduling still serializes the waves and retains the original differences in node-pair demand. 3.3 Calibrated Execution Selection No single execution path dominates across communication phases. RailBalance is beneficial when improved Rail utilization outweighs local redistribution, while permutation scheduling is beneficial when reduced incast outweighs the cost of additional communication rounds. These break-even points vary with traffic characteristics, motivating phase-specific execution selection. The selector uses three traffic descriptors defined in Section 2.2 : the average remote payload per GPU B B , the global source-Rail skew ρ g \rho_{g} , and the receiver concentration κ \kappa under the actual sending windows. Together, they capture communication scale, source-Rail imbalance, and receiver concentration for the current phase. After fixed normalization calibrated offline, these statistics form the lookup feature x = ( B ~ , ρ ~ g , κ ~ ) x=(\widetilde{B},\widetilde{\rho}_{g},\widetilde{\kappa}) . Phases with no remote payload retain the Native local path. Offline profiling constructs a calibrated anchor table. Each anchor stores a feature vector x j x_{j} and an execution path p j p_{j} . An alternative to Joint is retained only when repeated measurements are sufficiently stable and show a conservative advantage over Joint. This filters out decisions whose apparent benefit may be explained by measurement variation. The exact normalization, anchor-retention criteria, and resulting anchors are reported in Appendix A.3 .
